subject: Cushion mapping & throttle pathways — Nimbus commit

From: Samantha Reyes <samantha@syndicateai.com>

Subject: Dedicated compute ask + SLO for Nimbus pilot

Irene / Kimberly —

Thanks for the quick intro last week. As discussed, we need a concrete compute recommendation for our pilot + initial production phasing so procurement can draft terms. A few quick facts on our side:
- Workload: multi-turn clinical summarization + triage prompts (avg tokens/request ~350, median 280).
- Expected pilot peak: ~18 requests/sec; steady-state pilot 6–8 rps.
- SLAs: p95 latency target <= 250ms for user-facing summarization; p95 embeddings < 150ms (embeds are separate route).
- Model signal: we plan to run an optimized open-encoder 13B-ish variant (quantized) for production; pilot may try larger variant for eval.
- Timeline: procurement needs a recommended reserved slab size + a suggested burst lane and a short rationale.

Attached is a sample day of traffic and our procurement timeline (we've also included the legal contact). Can you map tokens/sec to GPU counts and call out headroom assumptions (peak vs. sustained, cold-start impact, fallback model pathways)?

Thanks — can we get a sketch by Monday so I can include it in the procurement packet?

— Samantha
Samantha Reyes
Head of ML Ops, Nimbus Health
Attachments: nimbus-workload-sample.csv, procurement-timeline.pdf
From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Dedicated compute ask + SLO for Nimbus pilot

Samantha — thanks for the data. I sketched a conservative compute mapping and a couple of operational paths (canary / fallback). High level first, then the numbers:

Summary recommendations (short):
- Pilot reserved slab: 6x H100-equivalent GPUs with a small shared burst pool (2 GPUs) for short spikes.
- Rationale: meets p95 <= 250ms at target model in our bench at pilot traffic, and provides ~40% headroom for traffic spikes and degraded model variants.
- Fallback: policy-based downgrade to a smaller quantized variant when queueing or CPU/IO signals show elevated latency; auto-route to hosted cheaper variant for non-sensitive requests.

Quick math (assumptions):
- Avg tokens/request: 350 (you provided).
- Pilot peak: 18 rps -> 18 * 350 = 6,300 tokens/sec peak.
- Observed perf: on our testbed, the chosen quantized 13B-like variant yields ~1,800 tokens/sec sustained per H100-equivalent at p95 ~220ms with batching optimized for 50–80ms batching window. (This reflects continuous batching + KV cache warm).
- GPUs needed (core): ceil(6,300 / 1,800) = 4 GPUs to hit peak without headroom.
- Add recommended headroom (40%): 4 * 1.4 = 5.6 -> round up to 6 GPUs.

Operational sizing notes:
- Burst pool: recommend 2 gated GPUs for uncommon bursts (short-lived spikes beyond sustained headroom). Burst should be billed as burst capacity or reserved but used as shared.
- Cold-starts: cold KV-cache warmup cost approximates an extra 20–30% latency for the first request stream; we recommend a short pre-warm step during deploys and a traffic ramp strategy for new model versions.
- Multi-model routing: route low-sensitivity traffic (analytics, offline summarization) to a lower-cost quantized 7–8B variant to preserve headroom on 13B.

SLA and throttling pathways:
- If request queue depth > 100 for more than 30s, trigger auto-throttle: reduce prompt length via client-side truncation guidance and spike to fallback model.
- Telemetry to watch: per-route p95 latency, queue depth, batch size distribution, KV hit rate, and GPU utilization.

I'll attach the Excel with the raw compute math and a couple of scenarios (pilot / steady-state / 3x growth). Want me to include a simple operator playbook for your SREs detailing canary steps and rollback triggers?

— Irene Choi
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Subject: Revised compute mapping + failover sketch (attached)

Samantha — quick follow-up after running an extra scenario with Karthik. Key additions in the attached PDF:
- Two scenarios shown side-by-side: (A) pilot steady 18 rps peak, (B) bursty traffic (hourly spikes to 45 rps).
- For spike case (45 rps -> 45 * 350 = 15,750 tokens/sec): core GPUs required = ceil(15,750 / 1,800) = 9 GPUs; recommended configuration = 9 core + 3 burst GPUs (20% headroom) OR 6 core + 6 burst GPUs if you want smaller reserved commitment with larger burst ability.

Operational playbook (excerpt):
1) Canary: deploy to 1 GPU in dedicated slab with traffic-slice 1% for 2 hours; validate p95 and KV hit rate > 90%.
2) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% over 48 hours with automated rollback if p95 deviates > 20% from canary.
3) Failure modes: if p95 crosses 350ms for > 10 minutes, route new traffic to fallback model and open an ops ticket via Console.

Fallback routing policy (implementation-level notes):
- Rule-based router in the control plane using: route_id, route_priority, latency_threshold, and a fallback_model tag. Example: route_summary -> if p95 > 250ms AND queue_depth > 50 -> fallback=quantized-8B.

Observability hooks to include in procurement packet: per-route cost/tokens, per-model p95, KV-cache warm metric, and burst GPU meter. We recommend a 24-hr lookback alert on p95 increase > 15% to catch creeping regressions early.

Attached: nimbus-commit-sketch.pdf (2 pages) and the updated token-runbook spreadsheet. Karthik also added a short note on quantization tradeoffs (see the last tab).

— Irene
